claims.text: A coupled MD and DFT framework will accurately predict temperature-dependent electrical conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The oxygen-containing bulk alloy has a disordered microstructure with distributed oxygen interstitials.
MD can represent finite-temperature lattice vibrations and anharmonic distortions relevant to this alloy.
DFT-based electronic-structure calculations can evaluate oxygen-induced defect states and their effect on carrier mobility.
Oxygen-induced point defects produce local lattice distortions.
Anharmonic atomic motion produces dynamic lattice disorder.
MD provides a time-resolved account of how vibrations and distortions alter the local electronic environment.
Oxygen defect states and local lattice changes modify carrier mobility and electron scattering.
Coupling MD with DFT captures temperature-dependent carrier concentration and mobility effects missed by existing analytical models.
Defect-induced carrier localization or freeze-out dominates conductivity from 0 to 200 K.
The conductivity curve will show a pronounced low-temperature decrease from 0 to 200 K because of carrier localization.
Thermal excitation and defect-related scattering co-occur from 300 to 1200 K.
Conductivity from 300 to 1200 K will exhibit smooth, thermally activated behavior aligned with experiment.
The predicted conductivity at approximately 300 K will be within 7% of the experimental value.
Existing analytical conductivity predictions typically assume a perfect, defect-free crystal lattice.
Perfect-crystal analytical assumptions reduce prediction accuracy when oxygen defects and dynamic thermal effects are important.
The coupled approach is expected to outperform static analytical models.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen and only within the stated 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
A deviation greater than 7% from held-out experimental conductivity at approximately 300 K falsifies the hypothesis.
